title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
This incident shows AI being used as a tool for impersonation and fraud, outside any legitimate deployment context. Scammers generated a fabricated news article using AI, placing real named public figures, a Reserve Bank Governor and a known finance presenter, in a fictional interview to lend credibility to an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform. The failure is not in a deployed AI product that malfunctioned, but in AI capabilities being deliberately applied to produce convincing disinformation at scale.

The content was designed to pass as journalism, combining real identities with fabricated dialogue and professional-looking presentation. ASIC's figures show this kind of operation is being run systematically, with tens of thousands of scam properties removed in a single year. Because the material is generated rather than recorded, there is no original footage to trace, and the volume makes manual detection impractical without automated countermeasures on the platforms where the content appears.

What is not established is who created or operated the Boulder Sparhaven platform, whether any individual has been charged in connection with this specific material, and how many people suffered financial loss as a result.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
A fake news article featuring Reserve Bank Governor Michele Bullock in a heated interview with ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler has become the latest example of an emerging scam trend. The fabricated piece promoted Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform, by creating a fictional confrontation. This incident demonstrates how scammers are increasingly using artificial intelligence to generate convincing deepfake content targeting well-known Australians, particularly Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Alan Kohler, and wealthy businesspeople like Gina Rinehart.

The Australian Securities and Investments Commission reports that AI-generated investment scams are rising rapidly and becoming more sophisticated. Last year, ASIC removed 19,400 scams total, including 7,051 fake investment platforms and 5,476 phishing attempts, representing significant increases from previous years. Scammers build elaborate webs of deception using fake news articles, reviews, and advertisements to lure victims. ASIC advises consumers to verify Australian Financial Services licence numbers through official registers before investing and warns that polished content and familiar branding do not guarantee legitimacy.
